blocks.text: Dear Mr. Wallace:

I am writing to set down, in the plain terms we prefer for such things, the basis on which our firm would take up the customer retention work that {{fact:f:E-2019-001.client}} has asked us to consider, so that once you have read this letter and, if it answers to the conversations we have had, signed it below, there is a single document to which either of us can return should a question later arise about what we agreed. I have been careful throughout to claim only as much as I am confident the firm can stand behind, in the work itself and in what we will charge for it alike, and if any part of what follows strikes you as promising more than that, I would far rather you put it to me before you sign than let it pass.
The Assignment as We Understand It

As I understand what you have asked of us, {{fact:f:E-2019-001.client}} has watched enough good customers leave over the last few years to want a considered look, from outside, at why they go and at what might be done to keep more of them, and you have asked us to build that look into a program you can actually run rather than a study you will file. Our work will move from an orderly reading of who is leaving and when, through the reasons that sit behind the pattern, to a set of recommendations on where retention can be improved and on how the effort to improve it ought to be organized and paid for. What the engagement does not take in is the running of your commercial relationships, which stays yours to direct, nor legal, tax, or accounting advice, on which you should keep relying on the advisers who ordinarily give it; where our analysis touches those matters we offer a reasoned business view and not a professional opinion in their place.
How We Would Go About It

Our manner of working is deliberate, and I hope you will find it plain rather than clever. We begin by listening, to you and to the people on your side who already carry a working sense of why customers stay and why they leave, and only then do we set down the few things the question truly turns on and build the analysis outward from them, so that every figure we eventually place in front of you can be traced back to where it came from. Where the evidence will carry a firm recommendation you will have one; where it will carry only a range or a caution, you will have that instead, because a recommendation that outruns what we actually know would be of no use to you and no credit to us.
The People Who Would Carry the Work

I will keep my own hand on the engagement and will read anything of consequence before it leaves the firm under our name, but the daily conduct of the work would rest with two of our people whom I would ask you to come to know. Deborah Jimenez, an Engagement Manager, would own the running of the assignment day to day, holding the workplan, chairing the working sessions, and keeping the cadence of the reports you receive; and Mary Parker, a Research Associate, would assemble the customer and market background that grounds the analysis and would keep the sources on file, so that no figure we cite is ever left without a home. You are welcome to reach me whenever you wish, though for most day-to-day matters Deborah Jimenez will be the quicker route to an answer.
Our Fee, and the Terms of Payment

Our fee for the engagement as I have described it is {{fact:f:E-2019-001.fee}}, which covers the time of the people named above through the close of the work. We will render invoices against that amount as the engagement proceeds, and each will be payable within thirty days of your receipt of it. The fee covers our people and their time and not the incidental costs of the work, such as travel or the reproduction of materials, which we will incur only with your agreement and pass through to you at what they cost us; and should the shape of the assignment change in any material way from what this letter contemplates, I will raise the question of the fee with you and we will settle it together before any further work is done, so that nothing ever reaches you on an invoice as a surprise.
When the Work Begins, and How Either of Us May End It

The engagement would begin on {{fact:f:E-2019-001.start}}, and I would ask you to expect it to run for something on the order of nine months, though I offer that as an honest estimate of the work rather than a promise about the calendar, since we will treat the assignment as finished when it is genuinely done and not merely when a set number of months has passed. Either of us may bring the engagement to an end on thirty days' written notice to the other, and if you should choose to do so you will owe us for the work properly performed to that point and for any costs already committed on your behalf, and for nothing beyond that.
The Confidence We Will Keep

Everything we learn about {{fact:f:E-2019-001.client}} in the course of this work we will hold in confidence and use only for the purposes of the engagement. That obligation binds every member of the team, it survives the end of our work together, and it reaches the fact of our involvement as fully as its substance. We would ask the same of you in respect of the methods and the written materials we place in your hands, which are the firm's own way of working and are meant for your use and not for wider circulation.
The Limit of Our Liability

We will perform the work with the care and skill you are entitled to expect of a firm engaged for it, and we stand behind what we do. We do not, however, govern the commercial decisions that {{fact:f:E-2019-001.client}} will in the end take on the strength of our advice, nor the conditions of the markets in which you hold and lose your customers, and so, save to the extent the law will not permit such a limit, our liability to you arising out of this engagement is limited to the fees paid under it.
The Law Governing This Letter

This agreement is governed by the law of the state in which our firm is established, and any dispute arising under it will be settled by the courts of that state. Should any single provision of this letter be found unenforceable, the remainder will continue in force, unaffected by it.

If this letter sets out the understanding we reached, I would be grateful if you would sign one copy where indicated below and return it to me, keeping the other for your file; once your signed copy is in my hands, Deborah Jimenez will write to you within the week to fix the first meetings and the opening requests for information, so that we can begin without delay.

To: Customer Retention Program engagement team
From: Deborah Jimenez, Engagement Manager
Date: 22 May 2019
Re: Kickoff -- Customer Retention Program for {{fact:f:E-2019-001.client}}

This is the kickoff note for the {{fact:f:E-2019-001.client}} customer retention program. The objective is settled and worth stating plainly before we open a single file: the client is losing good customers faster than it should, and it wants two things from us, an honest account of why and a working program to slow it, one its own people can run after we go. We hold the engagement to those two tests. Work that explains the loss without giving the client a way to act on it fails the second test, and a program the client cannot run once we leave fails both.

Our sponsor at the client is Joseph Wallace, the Chief Financial Officer, and he is our decision point on scope, access, and anything that touches the fee. Route client-side requests through him unless he tells us otherwise. The engagement began on {{fact:f:E-2019-001.start}}, and we are in the first days of it, so the early work is as much about getting the data and the access in place as about analysis.

The running of it is straightforward. I hold the workplan and chair the working sessions; Mary Parker carries the research and keeps the source file. The client has a status report from me at each reporting point, and every working session leaves minutes, so we all agree afterward on what was in fact decided rather than what each of us remembers wanting.

A word on the edges of the work is worth setting down now. We diagnose the churn and hand back a program the client's people operate; we do not run the client's commercial relationships or rebuild its systems, and where the analysis brushes against legal or accounting questions we give a business view and stop there. Anything that drifts past those edges I raise with Joseph Wallace before it draws down time we owe elsewhere.
Where the work divides

items: Churn analysis. Read the last several years of customer data to see who leaves, when, and how much they were worth. Mary Parker pulls the source data and files it against every figure we later quote.
Root causes. Interview the client's commercial and service people and test the leaving pattern against what they describe, so the reasons are grounded rather than assumed.
Retention options. Build two or three concrete ways to hold more customers, each costed and each described in terms of what it asks the client's staff to do differently.
Program design. Turn the chosen options into something the client can run itself, with owners, a cadence, and a way to tell whether it is working.

blocks.text: First moves are set. Mary Parker sends the client our opening data request this week, and I will hold the first working session with Joseph Wallace's team as soon as the initial cut of customer data reaches us. Nothing downstream moves until the churn picture is solid, because every later step leans on it. The first status report goes to the client at the end of the opening month, and I will keep this note current as owners and dates firm up.

What done looks like is worth naming too. At the close we hand the client a retention program with named owners, a running cadence, and a plain measure of whether it is holding customers, along with the analysis that stands behind each recommendation. If we cannot show why a step is there, it does not go in.
Dear Joseph,

Thank you for the sales and service extracts; they came through clean, and we are already into them. The churn read is taking shape, and the early news is good: the leaving is concentrated in a narrower band of accounts than your team expected, and a concentrated problem is a more tractable one. Mary Parker has the customer and market background largely assembled and is filing the sources as she goes, so every figure we later put in front of you will have a home.

Two things would keep us moving. We still need the contract-renewal dates for the mid-tier accounts, which were not in the last extract, and I would like thirty minutes each with the two account managers your note flagged as closest to the customers who left. If those introductions are easier coming from you, Joseph Wallace, I am glad for the requests to go out under your name; the sessions can be short, and we will come to them with specific questions rather than a blank page.

I would also like to hold a working session late next month to walk your team through the first read of the churn pattern. I will send two or three dates once the renewal data is in, so that we meet with something solid in hand rather than a half-formed picture.

Send whatever is readiest directly to me, Deborah Jimenez, and I will get it to Mary Parker the same day. I will keep this thread as the running record for {{fact:f:E-2019-001.client}} so nothing has to be chased twice.
Sincerely
Working Session -- Customer Retention Program for {{fact:f:E-2019-001.client}}

These minutes record a working session held to take stock of where the retention analysis stands as we come up on the midpoint of the engagement. We had reached the point where the churn data could finally speak for itself, and the session was given over less to gathering than to hearing what the data says and agreeing what we do about it. What follows sets down who was present, what we discussed, and the actions each of us left with.
Present

items: Deborah Jimenez, Engagement Manager, Calderwood Partners
Mary Parker, Research Associate, Calderwood Partners
Joseph Wallace, Chief Financial Officer, {{fact:f:E-2019-001.client}}

blocks.text: What the churn data shows

We walked through the first complete read of the leaving pattern. The finding that shaped the rest of the discussion is that the losses are not spread evenly across the book; they cluster in the mid-tier accounts in the second year of the relationship, and they cluster around a small number of service failures rather than around price. Joseph Wallace confirmed that this squares with what his commercial team has felt but never had the numbers to show. We agreed that having the pattern in hard figures changes the conversation from anecdote to evidence, and that the program should aim squarely at that second-year, mid-tier band.
The test Joseph Wallace set for us

Joseph Wallace was clear about the standard the program has to meet. He has seen retention pushes that ran on goodwill and a spreadsheet and quietly lapsed the moment the consultants left, and he does not want another. Whatever we design has to be something his own account managers can carry inside their ordinary week, without a specialist in the room to keep it alive. We agreed to weigh every option against that test from the outset, so that a clever program his people cannot sustain does not count as a candidate, and to describe each option in terms of what it asks those managers to do differently.
Where we still have gaps

Two gaps remain before the analysis can carry recommendations. The renewal-date history for a stretch of the mid-tier accounts is still incomplete, which keeps us from timing any intervention precisely; and we have not yet heard directly from enough departed customers to be sure the service-failure reading holds from their side and not only from the company's. Deborah Jimenez noted that both are closable inside the next few weeks and that neither puts the timeline at risk.
Actions

items: 1. Mary Parker to complete the departed-customer interviews and reconcile what they say against the service-failure reading, within two weeks.
2. Joseph Wallace to have his team supply the outstanding renewal-date history for the mid-tier accounts, within one week.
3. Deborah Jimenez to draft the shape of the retention options once the two items above are in, for review at the next session.

blocks.text: The next step is the departed-customer interviews; once they are done and the renewal dates are in, we can move from reading the problem to designing the program, and we will hold the next session to review the first options.
Status Report -- Customer Retention Program for {{fact:f:E-2019-001.client}}
Reporting period ending 30 September 2019. Prepared by Deborah Jimenez, Engagement Manager, for the client's leadership.

The engagement is on plan and within budget at its midpoint. The retention analysis is complete, the design of the program has begun, and nothing now open threatens the finish. What follows sets out, in order, the state of the work, what was done this period, where the budget stands, the work ahead, the decisions that rest with the client, and the one risk worth recording. The conclusion is at the top; the detail below supports it.
Where the work stands

We have passed the midpoint and crossed from analysis into design. The read of why customers leave is finished and was accepted by your team: the losses concentrate in mid-tier accounts in their second year, and they turn on a small set of service failures rather than on price. That finding matters because it points the program at a defined target instead of the whole book, and a defined target is one a small team can actually work. Three design threads are open against it, all three on their planned course, and the shape of the program is now clear enough to lay before your leadership at the next review.
Done this period

items: Churn analysis closed. The full leaving pattern was reconciled to the customer data and accepted by the client, with the concentration in the second-year mid-tier band confirmed in hard figures rather than left as an impression.

Departed-customer interviews completed. Mary Parker finished the interviews with lost accounts and filed the transcripts against the analysis, so the service-failure reading now rests on the customers' own account and not only the company's.

Program frame drafted. A first structure for the retention program was laid out, with candidate interventions mapped to the accounts most at risk and each one written in terms of what it asks the client's staff to do.

Measurement approach outlined. We settled how the program's effect will be read once it is live, using data the client already holds, so the client can judge for itself whether customers are being kept without depending on us to produce the number.

blocks.text: Budget

The engagement is billed against a fixed fee of {{fact:f:E-2019-001.fee}}. About half of that has been earned as of this report, which matches the share of the planned work now complete, and the burn has tracked the plan closely enough that no correction is needed. On the current projection the remaining work is deliverable within the fixed fee, and no further authorization is expected. I will flag it early if the design phase turns out to need more of the client's time than planned, since that is the one thing that could press the estimate.
Work ahead

items: Finish the design of the retention program and cost each intervention, so the client is choosing among options it can see the price of.
Build the measures that will tell the client whether the program is working once it is running.
Set out who on the client's side owns each part of the program, so it can be run without us in the room.
Prepare the handover materials, including a short operating guide for each intervention, so the client's team can carry the program on its own after we go.

blocks.text: Decisions for the client

Two decisions rest with the client before the coming period can run as planned. The first is who on the client's side will own each part of the program once it is live; the design can name the roles, but the people have to be chosen by the client, and the sooner they are, the sooner they can be brought into the design rather than handed a finished thing. The second is whether to trial the program with a single account team before taking it across the book, which is the course we recommend, because it lets the client see the steps work and adjust them at low cost before committing everyone.
Risk

One risk is worth recording plainly. The program leans on the client's account managers to carry the new retention steps alongside their existing load, and if that ownership is not settled early, the design will be sound on paper and hard to run in practice. We are addressing it now by naming owners as part of the design rather than after it, and by keeping each step small enough to fold into the working week. No other item now open is likely to move the target dates.

In short, the work is where it should be at the midpoint, the budget is in hand, and the one real risk is one the client is placed to resolve directly. I will bring the program frame and the two decisions above to the next review and can walk your leadership through them then.
Working Session -- Customer Retention Program for {{fact:f:E-2019-001.client}}

These are the minutes of the session we held to review the retention program now that it has taken close to its final shape. With the engagement in its later stretch, the work of the day was less about analysis, which is behind us, and more about making sure the program we hand over is one the client can actually run once we are no longer in the room. We record here who took part, what we settled, the one question we left open, and what each of us carries forward.
Attendees

items: Mary Parker, Research Associate, Calderwood Partners
Deborah Jimenez, Engagement Manager, Calderwood Partners
Joseph Wallace, Chief Financial Officer, {{fact:f:E-2019-001.client}}

blocks.text: The program as it stands

We took Joseph Wallace and his team through the program in the form it has now reached. It rests on three interventions aimed at the second-year mid-tier accounts where the losses concentrate: an earlier and more deliberate renewal conversation, a service-recovery step that catches failures before they cost an account, and a simple monthly read of the accounts most at risk. Joseph Wallace's chief concern was not the design but the load it puts on his account managers, and we spent much of the session on how to fold the steps into what they already do rather than adding to it.
What we settled

We agreed three things. The program will name a single owner on the client's side for each intervention, so accountability does not blur once we leave. The monthly at-risk read will be built from data the client already holds, so nothing depends on us to produce it. And the rollout will begin with a single account team as a trial before it goes wide, so the client can see the steps work and adjust them before committing everyone to them.
The question still open

One question we did not close, and did not want to close in haste. Joseph Wallace pressed on whether the earlier renewal conversation risks handing concessions to accounts that would have stayed anyway, and it is a fair point that goes to the cost of the program. We agreed to look, before the next session, at whether the renewal step can be aimed only at the accounts the analysis marks as genuinely at risk, so that the client spends its effort where the loss actually sits and not across the whole book.
Actions

rows: Turn the agreed design into the final program document, with an owner named against each intervention
Nominate the account team that will run the initial trial and confirm its lead
Assemble the at-risk account read from existing client data and document how it is produced

blocks.text: The next step is the trial. Once Deborah Jimenez has the final program document and the client has named its trial team, we will stand the first intervention up with that team and watch how it runs before we take the program across the book.
